title: Europe Pays 114 Euros for Gas With Storage at 75 Percent, and Washington's Russian Diesel Is Sailing Toward a Legal Wall
subhead: TTF broke 100 euros per MWh on Friday for the first time since 2022 as Qatar's force majeure runs to year-end, while the first cargo under Trump's diesel deal heads for New York with no named buyer and 12 senators demanding it be rescinded.

sections.heading: The Gas Crisis Is Now a Numbers Problem, Not a Headline
sections.body:
Europe's benchmark gas price at the Dutch TTF hub hit 101.82 euros ($114) per MWh on Friday, the first time it has traded above 100 euros since the 2022 crisis, according to OilPrice.com. The front-month contract jumped 4% in Amsterdam and was on course for an 8% weekly gain.

The arithmetic behind it is unglamorous and unforgiving. EU storage stood at 74.89% on October 29, per Gas Infrastructure Europe data cited by OilPrice.com, against a five-year average of about 86% for the season. Withdrawals have already begun in several countries, meaning the 75% mark is the winter's starting position, not a floor.

QatarEnergy extended its force majeure on LNG deliveries to the end of 2026 this week, removing contracted Qatari volumes from both European and Asian balance sheets precisely when heating demand starts. ING's head of commodities strategy Warren Patterson wrote in a Thursday note that supply disruption is 'creeping deeper into the heating season', and flagged unplanned Norwegian outages adding to the squeeze.

Patterson also pointed to the political calendar: the risk of renewed US strikes on Iran after the midterms. Markets are pricing a war risk that could get worse on November 4, not better.
sections.whyItMatters: A 75% storage fill heading into winter is the lowest buffer Europe has had since 2022, and the cheapest relief valve — Qatari LNG — is contractually closed until January. Every cold spell from now on is bought at whatever TTF the market names that morning.

sections.heading: Japan Takes the LNG Crown From China, and Both Are Buying Less
sections.body:
Japan will overtake China as the world's largest LNG importer this year, the first time since 2022, according to ICIS and Kpler estimates reported by Reuters and summarised by OilPrice.com. ICIS puts Japan at 62 million metric tons against China's 61 million; Kpler has 63 million against 62 million.

The flip is not a story about Japanese demand strength. It is a story about who hedged better. China built inventories early in the war and its underground gas storage was 80% full at the end of September, per Rystad Energy analyst Xiong Wei, letting Beijing step back from a spot market where Asian prices hit a four-year high. Japan, which cut gas-fired generation in favour of coal this summer as LNG got expensive, is still buying — and paying.

That asymmetry matters for Europe. Weaker Chinese spot appetite is the one thing this winter keeping a lid on competition for non-Hormuz cargoes. If Chinese storage starts draining faster than planned, Europe and Asia will be bidding for the same Atlantic Basin molecules in December.
sections.whyItMatters: China's storage discipline is doing more for European gas prices right now than any EU policy measure. That is a dependency Europe did not plan for and cannot control.

sections.heading: The Russian Diesel Cargo Nobody Wants to Own
sections.body:
The first physical shipment under Trump's October 9 diesel arrangement with Vladimir Putin is the Malta-flagged tanker Agioi Fanendes, which left Primorsk on October 22 with nearly 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low-sulfur diesel and is due at the Port of New York and New Jersey on November 7, per ship-tracking data reported by Bloomberg and OilPrice.com. Four days after the midterms. No buyer has been publicly identified.

The legal plumbing is the real story. Treasury's OFAC General License 135 authorises the sale, delivery and import of Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. But the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022 wrote the ban into statute for Chapter 27 tariff lines, diesel included, and a presidential waiver requires conditions — among them a peace deal accepted by Kyiv and advance notice to Congress — that have not been met.

Former State Department lawyer Scott Anderson, writing in Lawfare, told OilPrice.com that Trump can almost certainly waive the emergency-powers sanctions at will but that the statutory ban is a different animal, and that a court might not accept the administration's argument. Customs penalties can be pursued for five years.

Senators are already leaning on the private sector. A bipartisan group including Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Ron Wyden, Sheldon Whitehouse, Chris Coons and Elizabeth Warren, plus Republican senators, sent letters to bank CEOs, port authorities and fuel distributors warning that imports 'may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations', per RFE/RL. Twelve senators, six of them Republicans, had earlier asked Trump to rescind the deal.
sections.whyItMatters: A cargo with no buyer, arriving after an election that could hand subpoena power to the opposition, is the clearest demonstration yet that the diesel deal exists on paper and not in commerce. Whoever offloads that ship is volunteering for five years of legal exposure.

sections.heading: A Tanker Burns Near Khasab and the IRGC Contradicts Centcom on Mines
sections.body:
On Thursday a tanker transiting outbound 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman was approached by a small boat which attached two explosive devices above the waterline, per a UK Maritime Trade Operations warning cited by OilPrice.com. The blasts caused an engine-room fire that briefly disabled the vessel; the crew was reported safe, the fire extinguished, and the ship continued to its next port.

Separately, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi claimed on Thursday that four tankers had struck mines in the strait, and dismissed US Central Command's assertion that primary transit routes had been cleared, saying: 'The reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the air, on land and at sea, not on social media and in America's media war rooms.'

The claims cannot be reconciled from open sources. What is verifiable is that mine-clearing claims by one side and mine-strike claims by the other are both being advanced as negotiating assets, and that insurers price the dispute, not the truth. The tanker fire put Brent at $117 in Asian trade on Friday, before the front-month contract expired there.
sections.whyItMatters: Every incident near Khasab is now a data point in the Doha talks rather than a pure shipping event. The seven-day reopening clock reported over the weekend is being set against a corridor where a limpet charge can still reach a hull.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Stops Talking About Production and Starts Talking About Escape Routes
sections.body:
Aramco and the Kingdom are seeking partners to expand their strategic oil stockpile and are expediting alternative export routes, according to OilPrice.com's Simon Watkins, who reports that Saudi average output since 1973 is 8.295 million bpd and currently runs around 8 million bpd.

The concrete items in the push: expansion of the 1,200 km East-West Pipeline from the eastern fields to Yanbu on the Red Sea to 10 million bpd within two to three years; a redesigned IMEC whose eastern maritime leg now anchors in Oman rather than the UAE, letting India-bound cargo unload outside Hormuz before moving onto the peninsula's rail grid; and discussion of additional IMEC nodes through Egypt and Syria. Watkins cites planners estimating IMEC could eventually divert around 60% of container traffic that historically transited Hormuz, and a senior EU security source describing Greece as Europe's designated entry hub under an India-EU FTA and the US Senate's Eastern Mediterranean Gateway Act.

Treat the 60% figure with care — it is a planner's projection, not a measured flow. The direction is what counts: Riyadh is spending on redundancy after repeated strikes on Gulf infrastructure shook confidence in US protection.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia diversifying export routes is a quiet admission that it no longer assumes the strait will stay open, and that Washington's security guarantee is not something it can build a budget around.

bottomLine: Europe entered November with gas at 114 euros a barrel-equivalent and storage at 75%, and Qatar's contract supply is gone until January — that is the tightest starting position since 2022, and the market's only hope is that China keeps sitting out the spot market with 80% full caverns. Meanwhile Trump's Russian diesel arrangement has produced a single cargo, the Agioi Fanendes, due in New York four days after the midterms with no buyer and a five-year customs statute hanging over whoever takes it; twelve senators have already demanded the deal be scrapped. In the Gulf, a limpet-charge attack near Khasab and competing IRGC and Centcom claims about mines show the reported Doha framework is being negotiated against a corridor that is still physically dangerous. Riyadh's answer is not diplomacy but pipes — an East-West line toward 10 million bpd and an Oman-anchored IMEC — which tells you what the Gulf's biggest producer actually expects from the next twelve months.
sources: OilPrice.com, Gas Infrastructure Europe, ING (Warren Patterson), ICIS, Kpler, Rystad Energy (Xiong Wei), Reuters, UK Maritime Trade Operations, CNBC, IRGC (Hossein Mohebi), Bloomberg, OFAC General License 135, Lawfare (Scott Anderson), US Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, RFE/RL, US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Simon Watkins
